summary: Defines a way to mark SIP messages so they will be logged, aiding diagnosis of reported problems and regression testing. Since it is hard to predict the path SIP takes through interconnected networks, a mark lets the message be logged along the way.

eli5.summary: You put a sticker on a message that says write down where this goes. Everyone along the path notes it.

questions: how to trace sip calls across networks
what is the sip logme parameter
how to mark sip messages for logging
subtitle: A one-word flag in the SIP Session-ID header that tells every device on the path to log this call for troubleshooting.

tldr.problem: Operators need to examine SIP signaling to diagnose reported problems or test upgrades, but across interconnected networks it is impractical to predict the path signaling will take.
tldr.mechanism: A new logme parameter on the Session-ID header field marks a dialog as being of interest. Devices that see it log the full messages, pass the marker along, and echo it in responses.
tldr.outcome: Operators who agree to carry the marker can collect matching logs end to end, using the Session-ID's local UUID to line them up. The marker is disabled by default and must be authorized.

today: RFC 8497 is a Proposed Standard from November 2018, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 7989 and answers the requirements in RFC 8123.

sections.title: Why Mark a Call for Logging
sections.content:
When users have trouble setting up SIP sessions, operators often find the root cause by reading the SIP signaling. Regression testing after a software or hardware upgrade needs the same view. These checks apply to a small share of traffic, but they can cross several networks run by different operators, so the path cannot be predicted in advance.

RFC 8497 provides a way to mark a session as being of interest, so that SIP entities along the path can produce diagnostic logs. It meets the requirements for "log me" marking set out in RFC 8123. The marking is normally part of network testing controlled by the network operator and is not used in everyday user agent signaling.

The marker is carried in a new logme parameter on the Session-ID header field from RFC 7989. Implementations MUST implement RFC 7989.
sections.eli5: When something goes wrong with a phone call, the people fixing it want to see every step the call took. A sticker on the call tells every stop along the way to keep a record.

sections.title: The logme Parameter
sections.content:
The Session-ID header field was chosen as the carrier because session identifiers are normally passed through Back-to-Back User Agents and other intermediaries. The logme parameter adds no device-specific or user-specific information and MUST be passed unchanged along with the Session-ID, except where it is removed at a network boundary.

The grammar is tiny: logme-param = "logme", added to the allowed Session-ID parameters. The IANA registration lists it with no predefined values allowed.

The local UUID part of the Session-ID in the first request of a dialog doubles as a random test case identifier. This lets an operator collect all the logged requests and responses for one test. Several dialogs can be logged at once, told apart by that identifier.
sections.eli5: The sticker is just one word added to a label the call already carries. The call's ID number tells you which call the notes belong to.

sections.title: Starting, Stopping and Related Dialogs
sections.content:
Marking MUST start with the request that creates a dialog, and then applies to every request and response in the dialog until it ends. Marking that begins mid-dialog is an error. A device adds the marker either because it is configured to mark a new dialog (for example during a set time window or for particular called numbers), or because it received a marked dialog-creating request and keeps state so that the whole dialog stays marked. The trigger configuration itself is out of scope.

Related dialogs, such as those created by call forwarding, transfer, park and join, MAY be marked too, so that the entire session identified by the Session-ID is logged. The RFC walks through a call transfer. Bob's UA marks the first INVITE, Alice marks the REFER dialog, and Bob marks the INVITE to Carol. All three share the same test case identifier.

A SIP intermediary is required to copy the marker into forked requests. Logs SHOULD hold the entire SIP message and SHOULD use standard formats such as SIP Common Log Format or Libpcap.
sections.eli5: The sticker goes on at the very start of a call and stays on until it ends. If someone tries to stick it on halfway through, that is treated as a mistake.

sections.title: How Devices Behave
sections.content:
In the simplest case the originating user agent inserts the marker in the dialog-creating request and later requests, the terminating user agent MUST echo it in responses, and both log the marked messages if policy allows. If the terminating side sends an in-dialog request, it MUST add the marker and the originating side echoes it.

When an endpoint does not support the marker, a SIP intermediary close to it, such as an edge proxy or B2BUA, can be configured by the network administrator to mark on its behalf. Such intermediaries keep state about which dialogs are being logged. A Proxy-B2BUA SHOULD copy the marking from the terminating side to the originating side, and signaling-only B2BUAs SHOULD couple related dialogs and pass the marker both ways. All B2BUAs MUST mark in-dialog requests they generate themselves in a marked dialog.

Other intermediaries in the middle MUST simply log any marked request or response statelessly, if local policy allows.
sections.eli5: If a phone does not know about stickers, the nearest switchboard puts the sticker on for it. Everyone in the middle just writes down any call that has a sticker.

sections.title: Crossing Network Boundaries
sections.content:
Networks may be connected directly or through a peering network, usually under specific agreements. Troubleshooting is easier if peers agree to pass the marker unchanged. Because a marker may make an entity log the SIP header and body, the marker MUST be removed at a network boundary when no agreement exists between the peers.

The RFC shows several stateful cases using example call flows. A network can strip the marker toward an outside network so as not to trigger unintended logging there, then add it back to messages coming in for that dialog. A terminating network can likewise keep outside markers from reaching its internal entities and re-add them on the way out. Intermediaries that do not follow the RFC may pass the marker unchanged or drop it altogether, which is why end-to-end marking is not guaranteed.
sections.eli5: Before letting your sticker go into another company's network, you check that they agreed. If they did not, the sticker is peeled off at the door.

sections.title: Marking Errors
sections.content:
Two error types matter: a marker that is unexpectedly missing from a dialog that is being logged, and a marker that starts mid-dialog. Detection is judged per neighbor: it is an error if a neighbor sent the marker earlier in the dialog and then stopped. Entities that keep no state cannot detect these errors, and a plain SIP proxy simply forwards whatever marker it receives.

On a missing-marker error, a UA, intermediary or B2BUA SHOULD treat it as an error condition, MUST NOT mark later messages and MUST stop logging that dialog. Messages already logged SHOULD be kept. On a mid-dialog start, the entity MUST NOT forward the marker or log the message, and MUST NOT mark or log anything later in that dialog.

Some missing or mid-dialog markers are not errors, for example when a non-supporting endpoint never sends it, or when an intermediary marking on behalf of an endpoint adds it to a message sent toward that endpoint. For a SIP INVITE with a Join header, an aware entity that is already marking MUST NOT mark the new dialog if the INVITE carries no marker, and one that is not marking MUST mark the new dialog if the INVITE carries the marker.
sections.eli5: If the sticker suddenly vanishes from a call that had one, or shows up halfway through, something is wrong and everyone stops writing notes for that call.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Logging MUST be disabled by default on endpoints and intermediaries, and enabled only by authorized users. Permission MUST be limited to specific calls of interest in a given time period, and debug configuration MUST reach an authorized terminal over a secure channel. The marker is not sensitive in itself, but it makes entities log messages, so a marker inserted by mistake MUST be removed at the earliest opportunity.

Maliciously marking many dialogs at once could overload the entities that log. The number of simultaneously logged dialogs can be limited, and edge devices such as Session Border Controllers can screen out markers when no testing is going on. A SIP entity that holds logs MUST protect them.
sections.eli5: Writing down every call is a big job and could be misused, so it is off unless a trusted person turns it on for a short time.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Logs include all SIP header fields, so they can contain personal identifiers such as From, Contact and P-Asserted-Identity. The SIP privacy mechanisms of RFC 3323 can keep identities out of the logs, and temporary GRUUs can help. Using a provider-owned device with a dummy account for test calls avoids personal data altogether. Marking does not add new user data to SIP, but it may show that a given user has a problem.

If logged SDP carries sensitive attributes such as encryption keys, their values MUST be masked before the message is stored. Consent MUST come from the end user or the network administrator and is handled outside the protocol. Endpoints with a user interface MUST tell the user when a session is being logged. Entities MAY pass the marker through yet decline to log, based on local policy. Retention SHOULD be the minimum needed for each case, and logging ends with the dialog and its related dialogs.
sections.eli5: Because the notes might contain private details, people must agree first, the phone has to show that recording is on, and secret keys get blacked out.
